f.p: Department of Public Information, Government of Guyana
f.t: Akawaio is one of the nine Indigenous languages covered by Guyana's language revival programme, which the government moved to restart in 2021.

f.p: Minority Rights Group
f.t: Kapohn is the Akawaio people's own name for themselves, and like most peoples of Guyana's interior they are Carib speakers.

f.p: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana
f.t: Akawaio communities live in Guyana's Upper Mazaruni area and along the Barama, Upper Pomeroon, Wenamu and Upper Cuyuni rivers.

n.l: Upper Mazaruni area and nearby river valleys of western Guyana, with Akawaio also counted in Venezuela's census

f.p: Minority Rights Group
f.t: Census counts put the Barí at about 2,841 people in Venezuela in 2011 and 3,018 in Colombia in 2018.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia
f.t: Barí live in the foothills of Colombia's Serranía de los Motilones along the Catatumbo and Oro rivers, with settlements also in Zulia state, Venezuela.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia
f.t: The Barí language, of the Chibcha family, is being passed on to new generations and has speakers of all ages.

n.l: Serranía de los Motilones and the Catatumbo and Oro river basins in Norte de Santander, Colombia, and Zulia state, Venezuela

f.p: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane
f.t: France recognizes Parikwaki, the Parikwene language, as one of the languages of France spoken in French Guiana.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: The Parikwene speak Parikwaki, a language of the Arawak family; their own name means 'the people of the river of the middle'.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: Parikwene families have villages in both Brazil and French Guiana and travel across the border often to visit kin and to trade.

n.l: The Urukauá River in the Uaçá basin of Amapá, Brazil, and Saint-Georges-de-l'Oyapock, Cayenne and the lower Oyapock in French Guiana

f.p: Cultural Survival
f.t: Chenapou is the Patamona village closest to Kaieteur National Park, and Patamona communities hunt, fish and gather plants in the lands around Kaieteur.

f.p: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana
f.t: Patamona communities live mainly in the North Pakaraima Mountains of Guyana, with others in the South Pakaraimas and the Essequibo region.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: Like their Ingarikó relatives, the Patamona use Kapon as a self-designation in the border region shared by Guyana, Brazil and Venezuela.

n.l: North and South Pakaraima Mountains and the Essequibo region of Guyana, including villages near Kaieteur Falls

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE), Venezuela
f.t: In Venezuela's 2011 census, where people self-identified, the Pemón made up about 4.2 percent of the country's Indigenous population.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: Taurepang, Arekuna and Kamarakoto communities share the self-name Pemon, a word meaning 'people' or 'us'.

f.p: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana
f.t: In Guyana, Arekuna communities live on the banks of the Kamarang River.

n.l: Savannas of southeastern Venezuela, the Kamarang River area of Guyana, and Roraima state in Brazil

f.p: National Trust of Trinidad and Tobago
f.t: The community works to pass its culture on to younger generations and the wider public, serving as cultural ambassadors for Trinidad's First Peoples.

f.p: Ministry of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs, Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago
f.t: Trinidad and Tobago's government names the Santa Rosa First Peoples Community among the country's own Indigenous groups and holds a Day of Recognition every October 14.

f.p: National Trust of Trinidad and Tobago
f.t: The community celebrates its heritage as descendants of Trinidad's Nepoyo and Carinepogoto peoples, with a week of public cultural events each October.

f.p: Smithsonian Institution (National Museum of the American Indian and Smithsonian Latino Center)
f.t: Over about four decades a Taíno movement has grown in Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico, as more families and groups affirm their Native ancestry.

f.p: Smithsonian Magazine (Smithsonian Institution)
f.t: Taíno community groups take part in language research, including tracing the Taíno roots of everyday words such as hurricane, hammock and tobacco.

f.p: Smithsonian Magazine (Smithsonian Institution)
f.t: In the New York area, the Arawak Mountain Singers formed in 1991 and became active on the powwow circuit, one of several Taíno heritage groups in the diaspora.

n.l: Puerto Rico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and other islands of the Greater Antilles, and diaspora communities in the United States

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: In Brazil the Tiriyó share the Tumucumaque Indigenous Park, ratified in 1997 and covering about 3.07 million hectares, with neighboring peoples.

f.p: Vereniging van Inheemse Dorpshoofden in Suriname (VIDS)
f.t: Suriname's association of Indigenous village leaders counts the Trio among the country's four large Indigenous peoples, living mainly in the south.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: In their own language the Tarëno say Wü Tarëno, 'I am Tarëno', meaning 'I am from here'; the names Trio and Tiriyó came from outsiders.

n.l: Southern Suriname along the Sipaliwini, Tapanahony and Paloemeu rivers, and the Tumucumaque Indigenous Park in Pará, Brazil

f.p: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane
f.t: France lists Teko, formerly called Émerillon, among French Guiana's six Amerindian languages recognized as languages of France.

f.p: Parc amazonien de Guyane
f.t: Teko live in both river basins of southern French Guiana, at Cayodé on the upper Maroni and at Camopi on the Oyapock.

f.p: Parc amazonien de Guyane
f.t: Teko and Wayãpi are the two Tupi-Guarani languages spoken in the Amazonian Park of French Guiana, where Wayana belongs to the Carib family.

n.l: Camopi on the Oyapock River and Cayodé on the upper Maroni, French Guiana

f.p: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela
f.t: In 2020 Uwottüja communities of the Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers met at Pendare and declared themselves guardians of their territory.

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE), Venezuela
f.t: Venezuela's statistics institute notes that Piaroa is still used instead of the people's own name, Wótüja, a word non-Indigenous speakers find hard to say and that communities spell in several ways.

f.p: Pueblo Indígena Uwottüja, published by the Observatorio de Ecología Política de Venezuela
f.t: The Uwottüja held their first congress as a people in 1984, uniting around the defense of their ancestral lands 'like one churuata, with one voice'.

n.l: The Autana, Cuao, Sipapo and Guayapo rivers and the middle Orinoco, Amazonas state, Venezuela

f.p: Protected Areas Commission, Guyana
f.t: In 2007 the Wai Wai of Kanashen in southern Guyana made their titled forest a Community Owned Conservation Area; in 2017 it became a national protected area.

f.p: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana
f.t: Guyana's Ministry of Amerindian Affairs describes the Wai Wai as expert weavers and bead designers, and skilled builders who raised the landmark Umana Yana.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: Waiwai, a Carib-family language, is the main language in Waiwai communities in Brazil, and most young people born there speak it.

n.l: Kanashen in the far south of Guyana, and Indigenous lands in Pará, Amazonas and Roraima states, Brazil

f.p: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage
f.t: UNESCO lists the oral and graphic expressions of the Wajãpi, including the kusiwa graphic art, on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: In 1994 the Wajãpi began demarcating their own Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and founded the Council of Wajãpi Villages, known as Apina.

f.p: Parc amazonien de Guyane
f.t: In French Guiana the Wayãpi live along the middle and upper Oyapock River.

n.l: Wajãpi Indigenous Land in Amapá, Brazil, and the middle and upper Oyapock River in French Guiana

f.p: Ministry of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs, Government of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago
f.t: Trinidad and Tobago's government names the Warao Nation of Trinidad and Tobago among the country's own Indigenous groups.

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE), Venezuela
f.t: In Venezuela's 2011 census, where people self-identified, the Warao made up about 6.7 percent of the country's Indigenous population.

f.p: Ministry of Amerindian Affairs, Government of Guyana
f.t: In Guyana, where the name is spelled Warrau, Warao communities live in the wetlands of the North West District along the Barima and Pomeroon rivers.

n.l: Orinoco Delta of Venezuela, the North West District of Guyana, and communities in Trinidad and Tobago

f.p: Ministère de la Culture, Direction des affaires culturelles de Guyane
f.t: France recognizes Wayana as one of six Amerindian languages of French Guiana with the status of a language of France.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: Among younger people on Brazil's East Paru River, the Wayana language has gained great prestige.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: Wayana live where three countries meet: on the upper Maroni and its Tampok and Marouini tributaries in French Guiana, in southern Suriname and in Brazil.

n.l: Upper Maroni River and its tributaries in French Guiana, the Tapanahony and Paloemeu rivers in Suriname, and the East Paru River in Pará, Brazil

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE), Venezuela
f.t: The name Ye'kwana, which the people use for themselves, entered Venezuela's census in 1982 and has almost fully replaced the outside name Makiritare.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: Among themselves the Ye'kwana use So'to, meaning 'people', while Ye'kwana can be translated as 'canoe people'.

f.p: Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Indigenous Peoples in Brazil
f.t: In Brazil, the three Ye'kwana communities on the Auaris and Uraricoera rivers lie within the Yanomami Indigenous Land in Roraima.

n.l: Amazonas and Bolívar states in southern Venezuela, and the Auaris and Uraricoera rivers of Roraima, Brazil

f.p: Minority Rights Group
f.t: Census counts put the Yukpa at about 10,640 people in Venezuela in 2011 and 3,610 in Colombia in 2018.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia
f.t: Yukpa, a Carib-family language, has high vitality: in most communities speakers use it every day and make sure their children learn it.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia
f.t: In Colombia, Yukpa resguardos are made up of settlements each led by a cabildo menor, with a cabildo mayor representing the people before the government.

n.l: Sierra de Perijá on both sides of the border: Zulia state, Venezuela, and Cesar department, Colombia
